findings.claim: For Edexcel Component 1 Section B, you will be given a quotation from the novel and asked to write an essay in response.
findings.truth: "Component 1" and "Section B" are banned strings in lesson fields. The sentence also omits the choice of two questions. Edexcel 1ET0 post-1914 British play or novel: ONE essay from a choice of two, each preceded by a short quotation, 40 marks.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1120-1130; CHECK_PROMPT.md banned strings

findings.claim: Which assessment objectives are tested in Edexcel Component 1, Section B?
findings.truth: The keyed answer (AO1, AO3 and AO4) is correct, but the question carries the banned strings "Component 1" and "Section B". Reworded to "the Edexcel post-1914 novel essay"; key unchanged.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md line 1130 "Assessment Objectives covered are AO1, AO3 and AO4"

findings.claim: AO focus: AO1 (analysis of language, form, and structure) - throughout.
findings.truth: AO1 on this paper is a critical style, an informed personal response and textual references. Analysis of language, form and structure is AO2, and AO2 is NOT assessed on the post-1914 question. The lesson was teaching students to write for an objective that earns no marks here.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 620-640 (AO definitions) and line 1130 (AO1, AO3, AO4 only)

findings.claim: For AO4, ensure your essay is well-structured.
findings.truth: AO4 is "Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation" - the 8 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks. It is not essay organisation. Same failure family as the sister Edexcel units that defined AO4 as evaluation.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 625-650

findings.claim: “Whoever saw her, saw her next” - used as the curse quotation in a heading, a key fact, a takeaway, a knowledge check, a flashcard and two practice stems across lessons 4 and 7, and listed as an essential quotation to memorise.
findings.truth: The phrase is not in the novel. Samuel Daily's real words are "In some violent or dreadful circumstance, a child has died." All occurrences replaced with the verified line; the knowledge-check key stays at index 2.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: "In some violent or dreadful circumstance, a child has died" matches ~10 editions of the novel and the Mallatratt play; "whoever saw her, saw her next" returns no match in any book. https://openlibrary.org/search/inside?q=%22In+some+violent+or+dreadful+circumstance%2C+a+child+has+died%22

findings.claim: “I was young, I was sure of myself.” - quoted in lessons 1, 2, 5 and 7, in three practice stems, three flashcards and the memorisation list.
findings.truth: Not in the novel. Replaced with the verified line "I did not believe in ghosts. Or rather, until this day, I had not done so."
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: the phrase returns no match in any book; "I did not believe in ghosts. Or rather, until this day" matches every edition of the novel.

findings.claim: “They have learned to live with it”, attributed to Sam Daily - used in lessons 1, 2 and 7, in three practice stems, a fill-in knowledge check, a matching pair, two flashcards and the memorisation list.
findings.truth: Not in the novel and not a line Daily speaks. Replaced by paraphrase in prose, by "In some violent or dreadful circumstance, a child has died" in the exam stems, and by the verified "a desperate, yearning malevolence" in the memorisation list.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: "learned to live with it" + "Eel Marsh" and + "Crythin Gifford" both return no match; "desperate, yearning malevolence" matches 11 editions.

findings.claim: “I had never been in a place that so immediately and so forcefully affected me” - quoted in lesson 3, in two practice stems, a flashcard and the memorisation list.
findings.truth: Not in the novel. Replaced with the verified chapter 5 line "Suddenly conscious of the cold and the extreme bleakness and eeriness of the spot."
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: "so immediately and so forcefully affected me" returns no match; "conscious of the cold and the extreme bleakness and eeriness of the spot" matches 9 editions.

findings.claim: “A tall woman, dressed in deepest black” - the first-sighting quotation in lessons 2, 5 and 7, two practice stems and two flashcards.
findings.truth: The compound is invented. The novel reads "She was dressed in deepest black, in the style of full mourning that had rather gone out of fashion"; the woman is not called tall. Trimmed to “dressed in deepest black”, which is verbatim. “A wasted face” is left alone - no contrary wording was found.
findings.evidence: Shmoop appearances quotes (4.40) "She was dressed in deepest black, in the style of [full mourning]"; Open Library search-inside: "a tall woman, dressed in deepest black" returns no match in any book.

findings.claim: Narrator hindsight phrases quoted as text: “I had not the least idea”, “how little I understood” (L2), “I did not know then what I know now”, “if only I had turned back”, “I did not then know” (L6, including a flashcard answer and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: None of these returns a match. Rewritten as statements about the retrospective narration; the flashcard now carries the verified "I did not believe in ghosts" line.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: "how little I understood" + "Eel Marsh", "if only I had turned back" + "Crythin", "I did not then know" + "Eel Marsh House" all return no match.

findings.claim: the accident that killed Nathaniel (Jennet's son, referred to as Nathaniel in the novel rather than Nathaniel Drablow)
findings.truth: False. The boy was legally adopted by the Drablows and the death certificate Kipps finds names him Nathaniel Drablow. The parenthetical also contradicts this lesson's own flashcards, which say "Nathaniel Drablow's". Parenthetical removed.
findings.evidence: LitCharts chapter 11 summary: "Nathaniel Drablow (surname confirmed via death certificate)"; https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-woman-in-black/chapter-11-a-packet-of-letters

findings.claim: The child, the driver, and the horse were all drowned.
findings.truth: The death certificates record Nathaniel Drablow and the nursemaid Rose Judd, both by drowning - the nursemaid is missing from the lesson entirely. The driver was Keckwick's father, and study sources have him surviving the accident, so listing the driver among the dead is not safe. Narrowed to the two deaths the text records.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside snippets from the novel: "that Rose Judd had also died by drowning", "Rose Judd, nursemaid; cause of death: drowning", "the pony trap and its driver Keckwick...' 'Keckwick?' 'Yes. His father.'"; LitCharts chapter 11: "Only Keckwick survived."

findings.claim: Their pony and trap crashes - Stella dies, the baby dies in hospital.
findings.truth: The child is killed outright at the scene, and Stella survives the crash and dies ten months later. The card reverses both facts.
findings.evidence: Novel, final chapter: "Our baby son had been thrown clear, clear against another tree. He lay crumpled on the grass below it, dead."; LitCharts chapter 12: Stella "dies ten months later".

findings.claim: The older Kipps ... His wife and child are dead.
findings.truth: Stella and their son Joseph are dead, but by the frame narrative Kipps has remarried - Esme Ainley - and the children telling ghost stories on Christmas Eve are her children, his stepchildren. Written as it stands, a student would say Kipps ends the novel a widower.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside: "Esme is Arthur's second..." and "A few months prior to this, I had met Esme Ainley"; LitCharts character list: "Esme Ainley - Arthur's second wife".

findings.claim: Through chapters 5 to 8, Hill escalates the horror ... Then, the rocking chair moves by itself. Then, Spider is nearly killed by the marsh.
findings.truth: The nursery and the rocking chair are chapter 9 ("In the Nursery") and Spider's rescue from the marsh is chapter 10 ("Whistle and I'll Come to You"). Chapters 5-8 run from "Across the Causeway" to "Spider", where Daily only lends Kipps the dog. Chapter references removed rather than restructuring the lesson.
findings.evidence: LitCharts chapter summaries for chapters 9 and 10; https://www.litcharts.com/lit/the-woman-in-black/summary

findings.claim: Every one of the 42 practice questions is labelled "40 marks - Post-1914 Essay" but its mark scheme runs Top band (21-25) down to Lower band (1-5).
findings.truth: The question is worth 40 marks (AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8). A 25-mark ladder miscalibrates every self-mark in the unit. Re-scaled to five equal bands across 40: Top 33-40, Upper-mid 25-32, Mid 17-24, Lower-mid 9-16, Low 1-8, and the bottom band renamed to the house ladder name.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md raw mark distribution, Component 1 questions 7 to 30: AO1 16, AO3 16, AO4 8 = 40

findings.claim: at a country fair on the outskirts of London
findings.truth: It is a fair in a large park about ten miles out of London, not a country fair. Too small to be worth an edit, and lesson 4's own flashcard already says "A park in London".
findings.evidence: LitCharts chapter 12: "a fair in a large park about ten miles out of London"

findings.claim: What breed of animal is Spider? - A small terrier - Sam Daily's dog.
findings.truth: The novel never gives Spider a breed; she is "the little dog Spider". The card asked for a breed and invented one. Reworded to what kind of animal she is and whose.
findings.evidence: Open Library search-inside snippets from the novel: "The little dog Spider had, somewhat to my surprise, slept..."; no snippet calls her a terrier.

findings.claim: "For Edexcel Section B" (lesson 6 exam tip) and "exam technique for Section B" (lesson 7 description).
findings.truth: Section codes are on the banned list. Replaced with "the Edexcel post-1914 novel essay" and "the essay". Lesson 7's description stays under 100 characters.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned strings

findings.claim: “The sound of the pony and trap” listed among the essential quotations to memorise, and used as a practice stem in lessons 3 and 6.
findings.truth: This is chapter 6's title, "The Sound of a Pony and Trap", not a quotation from the prose. Harmless to quote but it is not a line a student can attribute. Left in place; the surrounding analysis is sound.
findings.evidence: Novel chapter list, chapter 6 "The Sound of a Pony and Trap"

findings.claim: Stella and the baby are killed on "a beautiful, sunny day", and Hill therefore subverts the pathetic fallacy pattern. Repeated in lesson 6 prose, a lesson 6 knowledge check keyed to "It is a beautiful, sunny day", a flashcard and three mark schemes.
findings.truth: I could not verify that the novel describes the final afternoon as sunny; the summaries I could reach do not mention the weather. The keyed knowledge-check answer is still the best of its four options (the other three are a stormy night, thick fog and a thunderstorm), so nothing is mis-keyed. Someone with the book should check the opening of chapter 12 and either confirm the sunny day or soften the claim in lessons 4 and 6.
findings.evidence: LitCharts chapter 12 summary does not specify the weather; Open Library search-inside for "the sun shone" returns other Susan Hill novels but not this one - not conclusive.

findings.claim: For a modern-text essay, you will typically be given a short quotation ... Check your exam board's specimen paper for the exact format and mark weightings.
findings.truth: Board-agnostic placeholder on a board-specific unit. The format is fixed and known: one essay from a choice of two, each preceded by a short quotation, 40 marks, closed book.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1118-1132

summary: Five fabricated quotations run through the whole unit - the curse line, Kipps's confidence line, Sam Daily's community line, the marsh line and the "tall woman" compound - and they are taught as memorisation material for a closed-book exam, so they are the largest finding. The exam claims are the second cluster: AO1 is defined as AO2 work, AO4 is defined as essay structure, three fields carry banned spec codes, and all 42 practice questions are labelled 40 marks but marked on a 25-mark ladder.
